Organisms are divided into five kingdoms on the basis of similarities and differences: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

Monera and Protista

Monera: These organisms are made of one cell and their structure is very simple, for example bacteria.

Protista: Most of them live in water, for example amoeba and paramecium.

Fungi and Animals

Both fungi and animals cannot make their own food. They depend on other organisms or dead matter for their food.

lessons.title: Vertebrates
lessons.notes_html:
All vertebrates have a backbone in their body. They are classified into fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals on the basis of their characteristics.

Key Facts

  • The foot of an aquatic bird is the webbed foot — the foot with skin between the toes, which helps the bird swim. (In the book, the options for this point are pictures of feet.)
  • The cat belongs to the group of mammals.
  • A fish respires through gills.

Amphibians and Reptiles

Amphibians live both in water and on land, have moist skin and lay their eggs in water, for example the frog. Reptiles live on land, have dry and scaly skin and lay their eggs on land, for example the lizard and the snake.

Importance of Cartilage

Cartilage is light and flexible. A skeleton of cartilage makes the body of the shark and the sting ray light, so they can swim easily and move flexibly in water.

Stripes of the Zebra

The black and white stripes break up the zebra's outline in tall grass and confuse predators, so the stripes help the zebra hide from its enemies.

Large Ears of the Elephant

Elephants live in a hot climate. Their large ears help them release body heat and keep cool.

Pathogens

A pathogen is a microorganism that causes disease. It enters the bodies of organisms through air, water, food, animals (for example insect bites) and direct contact.

A mosquito bites an infected person and takes the pathogen into its body. When it bites another person, it injects the pathogen into that person's body. For example, the female Anopheles mosquito spreads malaria in this way.

lessons.title: Preventing Infections
lessons.notes_html:
Where Fallen Leaves Decompose Faster

Decomposition of fallen leaves will happen more quickly in the forest of hot climate. The soil there is always hot and moist, and microorganisms grow and work faster in hot and moist conditions than in cold and dry soil.

Excessive Use of Antibacterial Soap

Excessive use of antibacterial soap kills the useful bacteria on the skin as well, and the harmful bacteria that survive can become resistant. This disturbs the skin's natural protection, so the chance of getting an infection increases instead of decreasing.

lessons.title: The Flower and Its Parts
lessons.notes_html:
Four Parts of a Flower

The four parts of a flower are: (1) Sepals — green leaflets that protect the internal structures. (2) Petals — coloured leaflets that attract insects and birds. (3) Stamens — the male reproductive part, consisting of the anther (where pollen grains are formed) and the filament (which supports the anther). (4) Carpel — the female reproductive part, consisting of the stigma (where pollen grains adhere), the style and the ovary (which has ovules).

Labelling a Flower

Label the parts of the flower as follows: sepal, petal, stamen (anther and filament), carpel (stigma, style and ovary), ovule and pedicel (the stalk of the flower).

Reproduction is the process by which organisms produce new organisms of their own kind for the continuation of their generation.

Self-Pollination and Cross-Pollination

In self-pollination, pollen grains are transferred from the anther of a flower to the stigma of the same flower or of another flower of the same plant. In cross-pollination, pollen grains are transferred from the anther of a flower to the stigma of a flower of a different plant of the same kind.

Key Facts

Three States of Matter and Their Interconversion

The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. They can change into one another: a solid melts into a liquid on heating, a liquid evaporates into a gas, a gas condenses into a liquid on cooling, and a liquid freezes into a solid on cooling.

Evaporation

Evaporation is the change of a liquid into gas (vapours) from its surface, without boiling. Examples from everyday life: wet clothes dry in the Sun, water in a cup decreases when left open, and a wet floor dries after some time.

Condensation

Condensation is the change of a gas into a liquid. For example, water vapours in the air condense into drops of water on a cold surface.

Humus

The LED

An LED is a Light Emitting Diode: a small electronic device that gives light when electric current passes through it. It uses very little electricity and lasts long.

How a Musical Instrument Produces Sound

A musical instrument produces sound by vibration: when a part of the instrument vibrates (for example a string, a drum skin or air in a pipe), it makes the air around it vibrate, and these vibrations reach our ears as sound.
